extracted.intended_audience: aspiring entrants to The New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest / humor writers seeking to win the contest
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on producing and promoting a caption designed specifically to win The New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest, including writing style, joke type, audience targeting, and post-finalist vote-getting strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to win, not to be the funniest
rubrics_metrics.description: You are not trying to submit the funniest caption; you are trying to win The New Yorker's caption contest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor and victory are different matters entirely. If your goal is not to win the caption contest, why bother entering? Choose captions that maximize chances of winning over captions that merely maximize laugh intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for The New Yorker reader (isolated, introspective, urban ennui)
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Yorker reader is isolated and introspective, probably on the train commuting to work, suffering from urban ennui.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because readers are likely to suppress loud laughter in public, your caption should elicit, at best, a mild chuckle. First filter: Is it too funny? Will it make anyone laugh out loud? If so, discard it and find a less funny one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the gatekeeper (cartoon editor's assistant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assistant (who reads every caption and passes ~50 favorites to editors) is the first line of defense; getting past him is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know how the assistant thinks and exploit that perspective. The article notes the assistant is an outsider to the magazine's cemented culture (example: Farley Katz, ex-rollercoaster operator and telemarketer) — craft captions to match the stereotypes and sensibilities that the assistant uses to filter entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'theory of mind' captions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Theory of mind' captions require the reader to project intents or beliefs into the minds of the cartoon's characters (e.g., caveman: "Yeah, yeah—and I invented the ticket.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Theory of mind' captions are higher-order jokes and readily distinguishable from puns/visual gags; they have historically dominated winners (the article cites 136 of 145 winners, ~94%, as theory-of-mind). Aim for inference-based humor rather than literal labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puns, visual gags, and lowbrow/obvious jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns and simple visual gags (e.g., "It's a thongbird") are non-theory-of-mind and common in lower-tier humor sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of simian puns and cheap visual-label jokes that require no reader inference; these are unlikely to pass editorial filters for the contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep language simple and universally understandable
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common, simple, monosyllabic words so everyone gets the joke; nobody wants a joke that goes over their heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure references or complex vocabulary. Use words accessible to the magazine's broad urban-American readership so readers do not feel the magazine is 'above them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid proper nouns unless universally recognizable
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper nouns can alienate readers unless they are universally recognizable to urban Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excepting first names, only nine proper nouns have ever appeared in a winning caption (Batmobile, Comanche, Roswell, Hell, Surrealism, Tylenol, Bud Light, Frankenstein, Kansas Board of Education). If you must use a proper noun, keep it widely known and simple; otherwise avoid them and keep it lowercase and simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accessibility — do not make the joke go over readers' heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone must get your joke; avoid references that will leave readers confused or alienated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a caption requires specialized knowledge to understand, it's unlikely to succeed. Favor inclusive, instantly processable premises and wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the cartoon for appropriate themes (urban ennui, complacency) and exploit them
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for archetypes in the cartoon (e.g., 'a man in a cardigan holding a drink, yapping on his cell phone' as urban complacency) and build your caption to highlight those themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find resonant, contemporary social archetypes in the image and 'pounce' — align the joke with cultural observations that fit The New Yorker's sensibility rather than inventing an unrelated gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a finalist, run an aggressive viral marketing campaign to secure online votes
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest is decided by an online vote once finalists are chosen, so mobilizing voters is essential to actually winning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-mail everyone you know, create a Facebook group, call in longstanding debts, ask friends and acquaintances to vote. The author describes using personal networks (musicians, professors, relatives) and having 'no shame' about soliciting votes. Research other finalists: if they are unlikely to mobilize votes (e.g., 9-to-5 types), exploit that by campaigning harder.
